package_info.package_manager: N/A (applies to any Git-based repository, including npm, PyPI, etc.)
package_info.package_versions: N/A (applies to all versions where commit metadata is forged)
package_info.why_malicious: The entire repository is considered malicious because attackers manipulate Git commit metadata (timestamps and committer identity) to create a false sense of trust and credibility, luring developers into using potentially malicious code. This social engineering technique can be used to distribute poisoned packages or repositories under the guise of reputable contributors and long-standing activity.

execution_context.trigger: pre-commit (local repository manipulation before pushing to remote)
execution_context.file_location: Git commit environment (local shell or CI/CD pipeline)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: export GIT_AUTHOR_DATE="2010-04-01T10:00:00"; export GIT_COMMITTER_DATE="2010-04-01T10:00:00"; git commit -m "Fake historical commit"
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Before committing, the code sets GIT_AUTHOR_DATE and GIT_COMMITTER_DATE environment variables to arbitrary past dates, then creates a commit, resulting in a falsified commit timestamp in the repository's history.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior is suspicious because it manipulates the historical record of repository activity, making it appear as if the repository or user has been active for much longer than reality.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, commit timestamps reflect the actual time of code changes, providing an accurate activity history. Here, the timestamps are intentionally falsified to mislead users.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, developers may backdate commits for migration or archival purposes, but this is not standard practice and should be transparent.
key_indicators: Unusual commit dates predating repository or user creation
Bulk commits with non-sequential or implausible timestamps

execution_context.trigger: pre-commit (local repository manipulation before pushing to remote)
execution_context.file_location: Git config/environment (local shell or CI/CD pipeline)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
git config user.name "VictimUser"
git config user.email "victimuser@example.com"
git commit -m "Spoofed author commit"
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Before committing, the code sets the Git user.name and user.email to those of a reputable third party, then creates a commit, resulting in a commit falsely attributed to the victim user.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior is suspicious because it forges the identity of a trusted contributor, misleading users into believing that a reputable developer contributed to the repository.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, commits are attributed to the actual author, and users expect contributor lists to be accurate. Here, attribution is intentionally falsified.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Rarely, a developer may use a shared account or commit on behalf of a team, but this should be transparent and consensual.
key_indicators: Commits attributed to users who have no association with the repository
Contributor lists populated with well-known developers who are unaware of their involvement

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Before committing, the attacker fetches a .patch file from a legitimate user's commit to extract their email address, which is then used for commit spoofing.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior is suspicious because it is used to gather sensitive metadata (email addresses) for the purpose of identity forgery.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normally, fetching patch files is for code review or analysis, not for harvesting emails to impersonate contributors.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate use includes code review or patch application, but not for identity theft.
key_indicators: Automated or bulk access to .patch files for many users
Extraction of email addresses for use in git config

attack_chain.action: Attacker gathers email addresses of reputable contributors by downloading .patch files from their legitimate commits.
Attacker sets git config to use the harvested name and email, and/or sets environment variables to falsify commit timestamps.
Attacker creates and pushes commits with falsified metadata (timestamp and/or author), populating the repository's history and contributor list with fake activity and trusted names.
attack_chain.leads_to: Repository appears more trustworthy, increasing likelihood of malicious code adoption

attack_chain.action: Developers are deceived by the falsified metadata and may adopt or use the repository, potentially exposing themselves to malicious code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Potential compromise of developer systems or supply chain

behavioral_signatures: Commits with timestamps predating repository or user creation
Contributor lists containing well-known developers with no public association to the project
Bulk commits with non-sequential or implausible dates
Frequent changes to git user.name and user.email in commit history
file_indicators: No direct file indicators; detection relies on repository metadata analysis
network_indicators: Automated or bulk access to GitHub .patch URLs for many users
Unusual patterns of metadata scraping from public repositories
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor repository commit histories for implausible timestamps (e.g., commits before repository or user creation), and for contributor lists containing unexpected or high-profile users. Flag repositories with a high proportion of unsigned or unverified commits, especially those with suspicious metadata. Detect automated access to .patch files for the purpose of harvesting email addresses. Encourage the use of signed commits and vigilant mode to make spoofing attempts more visible.
